missions.title: TerraWatch-1 · Earth Observation Satellite
missions.nasaRef: Global Earth Observation & Environmental Monitoring Program
missions.historicalBackground: Earth observation satellites revolutionized modern science by providing continuous real-time monitoring of weather patterns, deforestation, ocean currents, and global climate systems. TerraWatch-1 serves as the inaugural flight for the orbital space program, certifying multi-stage ascent, orbital circularization, and precision payload deployment.
missions.scientificObjective: Inject the TerraWatch-1 satellite or planetary rover payload into Low Earth Orbit (160–350 km altitude), achieve orbital circularization, and deploy the payload to certify orbital spaceflight capabilities.
missions.missionBriefing: Launch the TerraWatch-1 rocket from the launch pad, pitch over into an orbital ascent trajectory, separate the first stage booster, ignite the vacuum upper stage, achieve a circular parking orbit above 160 km, and deploy the TerraWatch-1 Earth observation satellite.
missions.text: Mission 01 (Compulsory Program Milestone): Launch to Low Earth Orbit, achieve stable circular orbit, and deploy the TerraWatch-1 Earth observation satellite or rover payload.
missionPhases: Phase 1 · Atmospheric Ascent: Lift off from launch pad and clear dense lower atmosphere.
Phase 2 · Booster Separation & Second Stage: Jettison first stage and ignite vacuum sustainer.
Phase 3 · Orbital Insertion: Circularize orbit with periapsis above 160 km and apoapsis under 350 km.
Phase 4 · Payload Deployment: Separate and deploy the TerraWatch-1 Earth observation payload or rover package.
requiredCapabilities: Earth orbit with periapsis above 150 km

budget.basis: Standard qualification budget for Low Earth Orbit satellite delivery ($2.04M launcher construction, $3.5M mission total).

scientificData: High-resolution multispectral land surface mapping
Atmospheric aerosol and greenhouse gas concentration profiles
Global cloud cover and weather front tracking data
Orbital telemetry & microgravity payload deployment baseline

passCriteria: Stage 1 Ignition & Liftoff: Clear launch complex safely with nominal vehicle telemetry.
Booster Staging: Clean first-stage burnout and second-stage separation and vacuum ignition.
Orbital Insertion: Establish stable Low Earth Orbit with periapsis >= 160 km and apoapsis <= 350 km.
Payload Deployment: Successfully release the orbital satellite or planetary rover payload above the atmosphere.
Vehicle Survivability: Rocket and payload remain intact without aerodynamic breakup or surface impact.
failCriteria: Surface Impact / Collision: Vehicle or payload crashes into Earth surface or water.
Suborbital Propellant Exhaustion: Propellant depleted before reaching orbital velocity (~7,800 m/s).
Premature Payload Deployment: Jettisoning payload inside dense atmosphere (altitude < 140 km).
Orbital Trajectory Deviation: Apoapsis overshoots Low Earth Orbit ceiling (> 350 km) or periapsis re-enters atmosphere.
Loss of Attitude Control: Uncontrolled tumble or excessive aerodynamic pressure causing vehicle destruction.

missions.title: Apollo 11 · First Lunar Landing
missions.historicalBackground: On 20 July 1969, NASA astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first humans to walk on the Moon. The mission was the culmination of the Apollo programme, fulfilling President Kennedy's 1961 pledge to land a man on the Moon by the end of the decade. Armstrong's famous words — 'one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind' — were broadcast to 600 million viewers worldwide.
missions.scientificObjective: Demonstrate controlled lunar landing and return to Earth. Collect surface samples from the Sea of Tranquility. Deploy scientific instruments including a seismometer and laser retroreflector. Prove round-trip human spaceflight to the Moon.
missions.missionBriefing: Design and launch a multi-stage vehicle capable of reaching the Moon. Establish a stable Earth parking orbit, then perform a translunar injection burn. Capture into lunar orbit, deploy a lander to the surface, complete surface objectives, and return the command module to Earth orbit before re-entry. The lander must touch down at under 8 m/s to satisfy surface objective conditions.
missions.text: The definitive test of multi-stage rocketry and orbital mechanics. Launch from Earth, transfer to the Moon, land on the surface, and return. Requires a heavy-lift first stage, a capable upper stage for the translunar injection, and a dedicated lander with enough propellant to descend from lunar orbit and ascend back to rendezvous.
missionPhases: Phase 1 · Earth Ascent: Launch to Earth parking orbit (185 km).
Phase 2 · Translunar Injection: Burn from parking orbit toward the Moon.
Phase 3 · Lunar Orbit Insertion: Capture into a 100 km lunar orbit.
Phase 4 · Lunar Descent: Separate lander, powered descent to surface.
Phase 5 · Surface Operations: Touch down and complete surface objectives.
Phase 6 · Lunar Ascent: Lander ascent stage returns to lunar orbit.
Phase 7 · Earth Return: Command module departs lunar orbit for Earth.
requiredCapabilities: Earth orbit with periapsis above 150 km

objectives.label: Lunar Landing in Sea of Tranquility (< 8 m/s)

budget.basis: Planning allocations based on Apollo 11 Saturn V flight configuration ($4.35M vehicle, $7.0M mission allocation).

scientificData: Tranquility Base Regolith and Breccia Samples (21.5 kg)
Passive Seismic Experiment Package (PSEP) Lunar Interior Data
Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LRRR) Earth-Moon Distance Calibration

missions.title: Mars 2020 · Perseverance
missions.historicalBackground: Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater on 18 February 2021, a site chosen because it was once an ancient river delta — a promising environment for preserved biosignatures. The rover carries the MOXIE instrument, which produced breathable oxygen from the Martian atmosphere, and deployed Ingenuity, the first powered aircraft on another world.
missions.scientificObjective: Seek signs of ancient microbial life at Jezero Crater. Collect and cache rock and regolith samples for future return to Earth. Test oxygen production from the Martian atmosphere. Demonstrate helicopter flight on Mars. Characterise Martian weather and surface conditions.
missions.missionBriefing: Deliver a rover payload to the Martian surface. The mission requires an interplanetary transfer, a precise atmospheric entry, and a controlled landing. The rover must be deployed intact. Surface scientific objectives are conducted after landing. Vehicle design must balance launch mass, interplanetary delta-v requirements, and landing system capability.
missions.text: An interplanetary mission to deliver a rover to Jezero Crater, Mars. Requires a high-energy launch from Earth, a Hohmann-like transfer to Mars, atmospheric entry through the thin Martian atmosphere, and a controlled landing. The rover payload must be delivered intact. Mars EDL (entry, descent and landing) is the critical mission phase.
missionPhases: Phase 1 · Earth Departure: Launch to Earth orbit, then perform a Mars transfer injection.
Phase 2 · Interplanetary Cruise: Seven-month transit to Mars.
Phase 3 · Mars Orbit Insertion: Capture or direct entry approach.
Phase 4 · Atmospheric Entry: High-speed entry through the Martian atmosphere.
Phase 5 · Powered Descent: Throttle engine for a controlled landing.
Phase 6 · Rover Deployment: Release rover payload to surface.
Phase 7 · Surface Science: Conduct geological surveys at designated sites.
requiredCapabilities: Atmospheric entry at Mars (heat shield or parachute)

objectives.label: Powered Touchdown in Jezero Crater (< 6 m/s)

budget.basis: Planning allocations based on Mars 2020 Atlas V EDL stack.

scientificData: Atmospheric Entry Hypersonic Deceleration Telemetry
Mastcam-Z High-Resolution Ancient Lakebed Panoramas
MOXIE In-Situ Atmospheric Oxygen Generation Telemetry
Sealed Jezero Crater Astrobiological Core Samples

missions.title: OSIRIS-REx · Asteroid Sample Return
missions.historicalBackground: OSIRIS-REx (Origins, Spectral Interpretation, Resource Identification, Security, Regolith Explorer) arrived at asteroid Bennu in December 2018. On 20 October 2020 it performed a touch-and-go sample collection manoeuvre, briefly contacting the surface and collecting at least 60 grams of material. The sample capsule returned to Earth on 24 September 2023, delivering the largest asteroid sample ever collected by a NASA mission.
missions.scientificObjective: Return a pristine sample of carbonaceous asteroid material from Bennu. Map the asteroid's surface composition and structure. Measure the Yarkovsky effect (thermal radiation pressure on the asteroid's orbit). Assess the potential impact hazard Bennu poses to Earth in the late 22nd century.
missions.missionBriefing: Launch an interceptor spacecraft toward asteroid Bennu. Conduct proximity operations in Bennu's extremely weak gravity field (surface gravity approximately 6 micro-g). Survey candidate sampling sites. Execute a touch-and-go sample acquisition manoeuvre. Store the sample and return the capsule to Earth for atmospheric re-entry and recovery.
missions.text: A precision asteroid rendezvous and sample-return mission. Navigating near a small body in micro-gravity requires careful trajectory management — standard impulsive manoeuvres are too coarse. The touch-and-go collection requires extremely precise relative velocity control. The return journey must target a precise Earth atmospheric entry corridor.
missionPhases: Phase 1 · Earth Departure: Depart Earth orbit on an asteroid intercept trajectory.
Phase 2 · Interplanetary Transfer: Heliocentric cruise to Bennu.
Phase 3 · Rendezvous: Decelerate into Bennu proximity orbit.
Phase 4 · Survey Operations: Characterise surface from low Bennu orbit.
Phase 5 · Sample Collection: TAG (Touch-And-Go) manoeuvre at selected site.
Phase 6 · Earth Return: Depart Bennu and target Earth atmospheric entry.

budget.basis: Planning allocations based on OSIRIS-REx New Frontiers mission.

bonuses.label: Sealed Sample Return Capsule Earth Recovery

scientificData: Global 3D Radar Polyhedron Shape & Mass Density Map
OTES Carbonaceous Chondrite Mineralogy & Hydrated Minerals
Pristine Bennu Asteroid Surface Samples (121.6 g)

missions.title: DART · Planetary Defense
missions.nasaRef: NASA DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test), launched 24 November 2021
missions.historicalBackground: DART impacted the moonlet Dimorphos of the Didymos binary asteroid system on 26 September 2022, travelling at 6.1 km/s. It was the world's first full-scale planetary defense test. The impact successfully shortened Dimorphos's orbital period around Didymos by 33 minutes — far exceeding the minimum threshold of 73 seconds needed to validate the kinetic impactor concept.
missions.scientificObjective: Validate the kinetic impactor technique as a viable method of altering an asteroid's trajectory. Measure the momentum transfer efficiency from a spacecraft impact. Characterise the ejecta plume and crater formed by the impact. Demonstrate that planetary defense missions can be planned and executed on compressed timelines.
missions.missionBriefing: Launch an interceptor spacecraft and plot a direct intercept trajectory toward Dimorphos. No orbit insertion — the spacecraft is expended in the impact. Precision terminal navigation is required to hit a target approximately 160 m in diameter. The impact velocity and vector must be within acceptable margins to produce a measurable orbital change. Post-impact, ground-based observatories evaluate the deflection.
missions.text: A one-way kinetic impactor mission requiring extremely precise terminal navigation. Unlike orbital missions there is no second chance: the spacecraft must hit a 160-metre moonlet at the end of a 10-month cruise. Trajectory planning and correction burns during cruise are critical. Terminal navigation uses optical imagery to home on the target.
missionPhases: Phase 1 · Earth Departure: Depart Earth orbit on direct intercept trajectory.
Phase 2 · Cruise: 10-month transit with trajectory correction manoeuvres.
Phase 3 · Terminal Navigation: Autonomous optical navigation toward Dimorphos.
Phase 4 · Impact: High-velocity kinetic impact on Dimorphos.
Phase 5 · Assessment: Ground observatories confirm orbital period change.

objectives.label: Earth Departure Burn to Heliocentric Orbit

budget.basis: Planning allocations based on DART Planetary Defense demonstration.

scientificData: DRACO High-Resolution Dimorphos Terminal Impact Images
Didymos-Dimorphos Binary Asteroid Surface Geomorphology
Kinetic Impactor Momentum Transfer (Beta) Determination

missions.title: Europa Clipper · Ocean World
missions.historicalBackground: Europa, the smallest of Jupiter's Galilean moons, is covered by a smooth icy shell beneath which evidence strongly suggests a global liquid water ocean — potentially twice the volume of Earth's oceans — in contact with a rocky seafloor. Heat from tidal flexing by Jupiter's gravity keeps this ocean liquid. Europa Clipper will conduct 49 close flybys of Europa between 2031 and 2034, measuring ice thickness, characterising the subsurface ocean and searching for plumes of water vapour venting through the ice.
missions.scientificObjective: Determine whether Europa's subsurface ocean is habitable. Characterise the composition and thickness of the ice shell. Search for active water plumes. Map surface geology and identify potential future landing sites. Measure Europa's magnetic field interaction with Jupiter's magnetosphere.
missions.missionBriefing: Design a spacecraft capable of surviving Jupiter's intense radiation environment during repeated Europa flybys. The spacecraft must carry scientific instruments including an ice-penetrating radar, mass spectrometer, thermal imager and magnetometer. After arrival at the Jovian system, perform a series of close flybys accumulating scientific data with each pass.
missions.text: A deep-space mission requiring a high-energy launch, a 5.5-year transit to Jupiter using gravity assists, and careful management of a radiation-hardened spacecraft through repeated Europa flybys. No orbital insertion at Europa — the flyby approach limits radiation dose while still enabling comprehensive science.
missionPhases: Phase 1 · Earth Departure: Depart Earth toward Jupiter using a gravity-assist trajectory.
Phase 2 · Interplanetary Cruise: 5.5-year transit using Mars and Earth gravity assists.
Phase 3 · Jupiter Orbit Insertion: Capture into an elongated Jovian orbit.
Phase 4 · Tour Phase: Use moon gravity assists to lower orbit and reduce inclination.
Phase 5 · Europa Flybys: Conduct 49 close flybys over three years.
Phase 6 · Data Return: Transmit accumulated scientific data to Earth.

budget.basis: Planning allocations based on Europa Clipper Flagship mission.

bonuses.label: Close Sub-25 km Europa Radar Sounding

scientificData: REASON Ice-Penetrating Radar Subsurface Water Shell Profiles
MASPEX Neutral Gas Plume Mass Spectrometry
PIMS Induced Magnetic Field Ocean Salinity Characterization

missions.title: Lucy · Trojan Asteroid Explorer
missions.historicalBackground: Lucy takes its name from the fossilised human ancestor skeleton that transformed our understanding of human evolution. The spacecraft is on a 12-year journey to visit seven Trojan asteroids — the first mission to explore these primitive bodies, which are thought to be the leftover building blocks of the giant planets. The Trojans lead and trail Jupiter in its orbit, locked by gravitational resonance since the solar system formed 4.5 billion years ago.
missions.scientificObjective: Survey seven Jupiter Trojan asteroids across two distinct swarms (L4 and L5). Determine their surface composition, geology and colour diversity. Test whether Trojans represent a diverse reservoir of primordial solar system material. Characterise binary asteroid Patroclus–Menoetius before the main Trojan tour.
missions.destination: Jupiter Trojan asteroids (L4 and L5 swarms)
missions.missionBriefing: Launch on a trajectory that uses multiple Earth gravity assists to reach both the leading (L4) and trailing (L5) Trojan swarms — an unprecedented double-swarm tour. Each flyby is brief (minutes to hours), so instrument operations must be pre-planned and timed precisely. Solar panels must generate adequate power at Jupiter distances where solar intensity is 25 times lower than at Earth.
missions.text: A multi-target flyby mission requiring a complex trajectory with Earth gravity assists and tightly timed observation windows at each asteroid. Unlike an orbiter, Lucy flies through each target zone only once — data collection windows are unforgiving and cannot be recovered. Solar panel sizing is critical at Jupiter distance.
missionPhases: Phase 1 · Earth Departure: Launch into an elliptical heliocentric orbit.
Phase 2 · Earth Gravity Assist 1: First Earth flyby to raise aphelion.
Phase 3 · Inner Main Belt Flyby: Dinkinesh and Donaldjohanson flybys.
Phase 4 · L4 Trojan Tour: Eurybates, Polymele, Leucus and Orus flybys.
Phase 5 · Earth Gravity Assist 2: Second Earth flyby for L5 trajectory.
Phase 6 · L5 Trojan Flyby: Patroclus–Menoetius binary flyby.

objectives.label: Flyby of Inner Belt Asteroid Dinkinesh
Flyby of Main Belt Asteroid Donaldjohanson

budget.basis: Planning allocations based on Lucy Discovery Program multi-target tour.

scientificData: Dinkinesh Main-Belt Contact Binary Asteroid Imagery
Donaldjohanson High-Velocity Collision Fragment Spectra
Eurybates C-type Trojan Primitive Volatiles Survey

missions.title: Juno · Jupiter Orbiter
missions.historicalBackground: Juno arrived at Jupiter on 5 July 2016, becoming only the second spacecraft to orbit Jupiter after Galileo. Its polar orbit takes it over the planet's poles every 53 days, diving inside Jupiter's intense radiation belts for brief science passes. Juno has revealed Jupiter's atmosphere extends to depths of 3,000 km, that its Great Red Spot has roots hundreds of kilometres deep, and that the planet has a fuzzy, diffuse core rather than a compact solid one.
missions.scientificObjective: Measure the composition, gravity field, magnetic field and atmospheric dynamics of Jupiter. Determine the planet's water and ammonia abundance. Characterise the structure of the magnetic field. Image the polar aurora and atmospheric features with the JunoCam instrument.
missions.missionBriefing: Design a spacecraft capable of reaching Jupiter, performing a precisely timed orbital insertion burn to enter a highly elliptical polar orbit, and surviving repeated passes through Jupiter's radiation belts. The science orbit is 53 days per revolution. Each close approach passes within 5,000 km of the cloud tops. Perijove passes require accurate thrust direction and timing.
missions.text: A deep-space mission to reach Jupiter and enter a highly elliptical polar orbit. The key challenge is the orbital insertion burn: too little and the spacecraft escapes; too much and it enters a dangerously deep orbit. Each science pass brings the spacecraft within the most intense radiation environment of any body the game models.
missionPhases: Phase 1 · Earth Departure: Depart Earth orbit on a Jupiter transfer trajectory.
Phase 2 · Earth Gravity Assist: Flyby of Earth after 2 years to gain additional speed.
Phase 3 · Jupiter Approach: Fine trajectory correction burns.
Phase 4 · Jupiter Orbit Insertion: Precision burn to enter capture orbit.
Phase 5 · Science Orbit: Establish a 53-day polar orbit.
Phase 6 · Perijove Passes: Conduct repeated science passes over the poles.

budget.basis: Planning allocations based on Juno New Frontiers Jupiter orbiter.

scientificData: Deep Jovian Atmospheric Water & Ammonia Abundance Profiles
Polar 3D Magnetic Dynamo and Auroral Plasma Observations
JunoCam Polar Atmospheric Storm Cyclonic Dynamics

missions.title: InSight · Mars Interior Science
missions.historicalBackground: InSight (Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy and Heat Transport) landed in Elysium Planitia on 26 November 2018. Its HP³ heat probe was designed to burrow 5 metres beneath the surface, but Martian soil proved unexpectedly resistant. Its SEIS seismometer detected more than 1,300 marsquakes before the mission ended in December 2022 when dust accumulation on the solar panels ended power generation. InSight was the first mission dedicated to studying the deep interior of Mars.
missions.scientificObjective: Measure the internal structure of Mars including crust thickness, mantle composition and core state. Detect and characterise marsquakes. Measure heat flow from the deep interior. Monitor Martian weather continuously from a fixed location. Determine if Mars has a liquid or solid inner core.
missions.missionBriefing: Land a stationary scientific platform in Elysium Planitia — an equatorial plain chosen for its flatness, low wind speeds and optimal solar exposure. After landing, deploy the SEIS seismometer and HP³ heat probe. Conduct long-duration observations. Data transmission depends on orbital relay spacecraft (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter). No mobility after landing.
missions.text: A precision-landing mission delivering a fixed scientific lander to the Martian surface. Unlike a rover mission there is no mobility — landing site accuracy is critical. The lander must survive atmospheric entry and powered descent in Mars's thin atmosphere. Scientific operations span several years, requiring sustained power generation from solar panels in the Martian environment.
missionPhases: Phase 1 · Earth Departure: Launch toward Mars on a direct entry approach.
Phase 2 · Interplanetary Cruise: Six-month transit to Mars.
Phase 3 · Atmospheric Entry: Entry, descent and landing in thin Martian atmosphere.
Phase 4 · Landing: Powered descent to Elysium Planitia.
Phase 5 · Instrument Deployment: Deploy SEIS and HP³ from the lander deck.
Phase 6 · Science Operations: Long-duration seismic and thermal monitoring.

objectives.label: Soft Landing on Elysium Planitia (< 5 m/s)

budget.basis: Planning allocations based on InSight Discovery Program budget.

scientificData: SEIS Very Broad Band Martian Crust & Mantle Seismograms
HP3 Subsurface Thermal Conductivity & Heat Flow Gradients
RISE Planetary Spin Axis Precession & Liquid Core Metrics
